item.title: Two-dimensional liquid-like order in a confined population of swimming Eudorina colonies
item.description: arXiv:2611.09946v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Swimming microorganisms accumulate at boundaries, but the spatial statistics of the resulting layers are rarely measured. We report a population of colonial green algae, of order 71 $\mu$m across, that accumulates against the rigid upper wall of a closed 1-2 mm chamber and holds a two-dimensional non-contacting arrangement for about 105 min. The pair correlation function has a first shell at $r/\bar{D} = 1.73$, $g = 4.8$; a hard-disc null at the same area fraction reaches only $g = 2.1$, so the ordering is not excluded volume alone. Nearest-neighbour separation is $1.80 \pm 0.13$ diameters. The bond-orientational order parameter is $\langle|\psi_6|\rangle = 0.456$ against 0.385 for the null, only 36% of interior colonies are six-coordinated, and the orientational correlation $g_6(r)$ decays over 1.5 diameters with $\eta_6 = 1.31$ against the hexatic bound of 1/4: the arrangement is a two-dimensional liquid, not a crystal or a hexatic. Colonies execute a persistent random walk with reorientation time 1.4-1.7 s at Reynolds number $\sim 9\times 10^{-4}$. Breakup begins at 127 min. Thermal convection is excluded on Rayleigh-number grounds. Caveats: the length calibration is nominal rather than metrological, and this is a single population observed once. All data and code are deposited.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Tufillaro

item.title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.10691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher--Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.
item.dc:creator: Aythami Bethencourt de Le\'{o}n, Darryl D. Holm

item.title: Quantum entanglement as a resource for self-organization and stabilization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11175v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can quantum entanglement generate macroscopic order that persists after the entanglement itself disappears? We establish such a mechanism in a driven-dissipative bosonic lattice, where local entanglement enables transport that amplifies spatial fluctuations into extended Turing patterns. For the full nonlinear dynamics with noise and disorder, we derive rigorous finite-time bounds on pattern intensity for all admissible separable evolutions, allowing arbitrary classical correlations. Quantum dynamics produces pattern intensities beyond these bounds during both formation and stabilization under noise. The excess intensity also provides a lower bound on the accumulated transport contribution beyond the separable limit. We further introduce an environment that responds to emerging order by suppressing local coherence and activating classical transport. The patterns then persist as local entanglement is lost, with both stages arising from a single time-independent Lindblad equation. These results show how transient quantum resources can establish persistent macroscopic order, opening new directions for harnessing self-organization in nonequilibrium systems.
item.dc:creator: Kazuki Ikeda

item.title: A Bifurcation-Theoretic Framework for the Controllability of Emergent Intelligent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.11734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world intelligent systems must reconcile two demands: the adaptability conferred by emergence and the steerability required for accountable deployment. We show that these demands are governed by two distinct bifurcations on the same object and that, consequently, increased capability does not imply increased controllability. Emergence is a bifurcation of the capability variable $S$, with criterion $\Gamma:=\mathcal F'(0)>1$ equivalent to the existence of a unique positive stable fixed point of a self-consistency equation, following solely from the concavity of $\mathcal F$. Controllability is a bifurcation of the permission variable $c$, whose dynamics include an erosion term and exhibit a saddle-node fold with hysteresis as the gate criterion $\rho^\ast$ crosses unity. Three quantitative results follow: the critical exponent distinguishes families rather than classifying the transition; the gating-cost bound $K(M)\propto\log(1+M)$ grows with scope, not capability; and the fold threshold is $\gamma_c\approx4\mu\kappa$. Calibrated in both directions, the criteria reproduce the two-dimensional Ising transition, admit two true-feedback order parameters, and reject nine candidate quantities, supporting the conclusion that the order parameter is geometric rather than capability-related. Since permission cannot be endogenized and no deployed system has been measured to satisfy $\Gamma>1$ and $\rho^\ast>1$ simultaneously, increased capability does not imply controllability.
item.dc:creator: Hao Li, Shaowen Lu

item.title: The role of administrative costs in policies to improve cooperation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12343v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We use an agent-based model for studying policies of an abstract government to increase the level of cooperation. In situations where defection is the rational choice, agents receive a bonus if they choose to cooperate. The government taxes agents' payoffs from a repeated prisoner's dilemma game to establish a budget that covers the payment of bonuses, but also the administrative costs involved. We consider costs to identify cooperators, and costs to mitigate the consequences of defective behavior. Governmental interventions are fallible, i.e. cooperators and defectors are correctly identified only with a certain accuracy. Hence, the critical bonus needed to let agents cooperate depends on the accuracy, but also on the current level of cooperation. We analyze the cost constraints for the government to pay the critical bonus and different policies to adjust the accuracy dependent on the level of cooperation. We find that perfect cooperation becomes impossible. Instead, high levels of cooperation can be achieved with optimal adjustment policies.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Vaccario, Luca Verginer, Frank Schweitzer

item.title: The Weight Is in the Reading: Hidden States in Memristors, Memlumors, and Electrochemical Transistors
item.description: arXiv:2611.12706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physical synapses are routinely described by a single number, the weight, that is identified with a conductance, a current, or a luminescence yield. This identification conflates two different objects: the internal state that the device stores, and the signal obtained when that state is read. Building on Chua's formulation of memristive systems, we separate the state variable, which evolves with the excitation history, from the observation map that converts it into a measured signal, and we define the weight as the outcome of a specified read protocol. Three platforms show the consequences: a memristor, in which the same voltage writes and reads; a memlumor, in which light both modifies the state and produces the photoluminescence that reports it; and an organic electrochemical transistor (OECT), in which the gate writes and the channel reads. In the transistor, two states prepared by different histories give the same channel current at a specific drain bias and become distinguishable again when the bias is changed, while the stored charge persists and the gate current continues to separate them. Published experiments provide precedents: a drain-bias-dependent cancellation of the OECT transient, and trapped charges in perovskite memlumors that are invisible to conventional time-resolved photoluminescence but revealed by a read-write-read sequence. A synaptic weight is therefore not a property of the material alone but of the material together with its readout, and reports of synaptic behavior should specify what is stored, what is measured, and how one is inferred from the other.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Rivera-Sierra, Heyi Zhang, Daiki Nishioka, Takashi Tsuchiya, Juan Bisquert

item.title: Global Analytical Solution of the Identical Kuramoto Model for N=3 via Koopman Eigenfunctions
item.description: arXiv:2605.07360v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Kuramoto model is a paradigmatic model of collective synchronization in coupled oscillator systems. Although its mathematical properties have been extensively investigated, explicit phase trajectories from arbitrary initial conditions have been available only for the simplest case, N = 2. In this study, we provide a global analytical solution for the phase trajectories of the all-to-all coupled Kuramoto model with three identical oscillators (N = 3). We construct Koopman eigenfunctions from products of observables whose growth rates, weighted by the exponents, sum to a constant, and obtain a nontrivial constant of motion from the ratio of two such eigenfunctions. Using their explicit exponential time dependence, we reduce trajectory reconstruction to time-dependent quartic equations and recover the phase trajectories. The same construction also yields Koopman eigenfunctions for the Kuramoto-Sakaguchi model with arbitrary phase lag and for the N = 4 all-to-all and ring-coupled systems. These results provide a concrete example in which Koopman eigenfunctions are used not only to characterize but also to explicitly solve a widely studied nonlinear model.
item.dc:creator: Keisuke Taga

item.title: Scale-Dependent Collective Adaptation in Self-Amending LLM Societies: A Cross-Family Study of Emergent Governance
item.description: arXiv:2605.17510v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study group decision-making in artificial societies where the rules of play are themselves subject to collective amendment. Using the self-amending game Nomic, we compare multiple scales across two LLM families and find that collective adaptation does not improve monotonically with model size. Instead, both families exhibit a narrow mid-scale regime that supports sustained rule adoption, diverse amendments, and balanced consensus. Smaller models tend to remain rule-inert, whereas larger models often converge on restrictive voting patterns, and heterogeneous mixed-size groups collapse into veto-driven gridlock. These cross-scale contrasts persist under temperature perturbations and under a shift from unanimity to majority voting, although latent-state structure varies by family and scale. Hidden-state divergence alone does not explain collective performance: high representational divergence can coincide with poor behavioural outcomes. Linear probes reveal regime-selective coupling between latent vote-predictive signals and collective behaviour, but decodability is necessary rather than sufficient for adaptive play. Overall, the recurring regularity is non-monotonicity, not the particular scale at which the optimum appears. Self-amending games therefore provide a controlled testbed for studying collective adaptation in artificial societies beyond raw model scale.
item.dc:creator: Kazuya Horibe, Masaomi Hatakeyama, Gen Masumoto, Takashi Hashimoto, Peter Romero

item.title: Increased-order generalized synchronization in memristive neurons: dissipativity analysis and data-driven control
item.description: arXiv:2610.25164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate increased-order generalized synchronization between four- and five-dimensional memristive Hindmarsh--Rose neurons, focusing on the selection and stabilization of the synchronization map. An analytical construction combines a prescribed nonlinear map with adaptive control, retaining the memristive switching contribution explicitly in the error dynamics. Lyapunov analysis establishes asymptotic synchronization under uniform strict dissipativity and yields a switching-independent decrease estimate outside an explicit error neighborhood. Numerical simulations exhibit error decay beyond the sufficient convergence conditions. A complementary data-driven construction uses next-generation reservoir computing to learn predictors from uncoupled full-state trajectories and an affine synchronization map through dynamical consistency. The resulting sampled-data controller achieves small residual tracking errors without access to the governing equations. Relative to a reference map within the data-driven framework, the learned map reduces median control effort approximately eightfold while improving tracking accuracy. These results connect synchronization-map selection with conditional convergence guarantees and reduced control requirements.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Mustafi\'{c}, Marius E. Yamakou

item.title: A learner-free swarm approximates the explore-exploit equilibrium allocation: A self-organized attractor in place of reinforcement-learning machinery
item.description: arXiv:2610.25113v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) solves the explore-exploit problem by training a learner on reward; its multi-agent, resource-sharing form has an equilibrium allocation as its optimum -- the ideal-free distribution (IFD), the Nash equilibrium of a congestion game. We show a minimal swarm approximates it with no learner at all. We present a decentralized, learner-free method for this problem: agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a degree-normalized threshold cascade, and disperse as a patch crowds. The method drives the collective to the shape of the equilibrium allocation (pooled spatial matching slope 1.14, R^2=0.61) with no training, no stored parameters, and no reward in its dynamics; it reaches this as a self-organized attractor and holds it, re-finding it when the resources move -- though it reaches the shape, not the exact equilibrium, and stays measurably exploitable (Nash-gap 1.46). Coupling recruitment to movement causes the allocation: removing it collapses the matching (slope 0.006). Against Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) learners (feedforward, centralized-critic, graph message-passing, and recurrent) trained in the same sensing-limited environment, the method at zero training is the only arm left unbiased w.r.t. the IFD gradient (slope ~1, CI containing 1, vs learners 0.69-0.97, all under-concentrating) and ties the best learner's harvest where resource is clustered, while the learner collects more where resource is scarce (0.33 vs 0.22) and holds a tighter per-capita intake. Learning buys precision and transfer across reward structures, not a better allocation shape. A companion paper develops the mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Galen J. Wilkerson
